title: Structured logging without secrets
summary: Message templates instead of interpolated strings, positional binding of values to placeholders, what each log level is for, scopes that carry a correlation id through a request, and keeping passwords, tokens, bodies, connection strings and personal data out of logs with an allow-list at the boundary.
lesson:
## Message templates, not interpolated strings

A log call takes a message template with named placeholders and the values as separate arguments:

```csharp
logger.LogInformation("Order {OrderId} shipped to {Country}", order.Id, order.Country);
```

The provider receives the template text unchanged plus one property per placeholder, so a log store can show every line of that template together and answer `OrderId = 42`. Placeholders bind to the arguments in order: the names in braces label the properties, and the logger never sees your variable names. An interpolated string, `$"Order {order.Id} shipped"`, is finished before the call, so the template is the rendered text, a new template for every order, with no properties to query.

## Levels say who must read the line

The levels, lowest first: `Trace`, `Debug`, `Information`, `Warning`, `Error`, `Critical`. `Information` records the normal flow (an order placed, a job finished). `Warning` is something unexpected that the code handled: a retry that then worked, a fallback, a slow dependency. `Error` is one operation that failed and needs a look. `Critical` means the app or a whole dependency is down. The ASP.NET Core templates set `"Default": "Information"` and `"Microsoft.AspNetCore": "Warning"` in `appsettings.json`, so `Debug` lines are dropped in production unless someone lowers the minimum for one category.

## Scopes carry the correlation id

A correlation id ties together every line of one request. Middleware reads it from a header such as `X-Correlation-ID` (or generates one), echoes it in the response, and opens a scope around the rest of the pipeline:

```csharp
using (logger.BeginScope(new Dictionary<string, object> { ["CorrelationId"] = correlationId }))
{
    await next(context);
}
```

The scope lives in an async-local slot, so it follows the request across `await` and into every class that logs during it, until the `using` ends. A provider shows scope values only when it supports scopes, and the console formatter prints them only with `IncludeScopes = true`.

## What never goes into a log

Logs are copied to other systems, kept for months and read by many people, so a secret in a log is a leaked secret. Never log passwords (a wrong password is often a typo of the right one), bearer tokens, API keys, cookies, connection strings or whole request and response bodies. Personal data (email, name, address, IP) needs a reason and a retention rule; a stable user id usually does the job: a failed sign-in line needs the user id and a reason such as `bad-password`, nothing more. Logging an object is a trap: a record's `ToString()` prints every property, so `{Request}` with a `LoginRequest(string Email, string Password)` writes the password. For a connection string, log the server and database names you parsed from it.

## Redact at the boundary: allow-list what you log

Decide at the edge what may be written, not after the fact in the log store. A deny-list hides only the names someone thought of; the day a partner sends `X-Api-Key`, it is logged in clear text. An allow-list logs known-safe fields and marks the rest. ASP.NET Core's HTTP logging works that way: it logs request and response headers but no bodies by default, and any header not in `RequestHeaders` or `ResponseHeaders` is written as `[Redacted]`. Log a body's length instead of its content.

## Exceptions and hot paths

Pass the exception as the first argument, `logger.LogError(ex, "Refund {RefundId} failed", refundId)`, so the provider stores its type, message and stack trace in the exception field. Passing `ex` as one more template argument does not set that field. Arguments are evaluated before the logger checks the level, so an expensive argument runs and its entry is then dropped; guard it with `logger.IsEnabled(LogLevel.Debug)`. On hot paths, the `[LoggerMessage]` source generator writes the logging method for you: it checks the level before boxing anything, and it binds placeholders to parameter names at compile time, so a renamed parameter is a build error instead of a silently wrong property.

```csharp
[LoggerMessage(Level = LogLevel.Warning, Message = "Retry {Attempt} for order {OrderId}")]
static partial void RetryingOrder(ILogger logger, int orderId, int attempt);
```

quiz.prompt: `logger.LogInformation($"Order {orderId} shipped")` prints the right text. What does it lose next to `logger.LogInformation("Order {OrderId} shipped", orderId)`?
choices: Nothing, since both lines produce the same text and properties
An OrderId property, and one template shared by every order
Its log level, which an interpolated string resets to Debug
Thread safety, since the string is built in a shared buffer
quiz.explanation: An interpolated string is finished before the call, so the provider receives the rendered text as its template: no property to query with OrderId = 42, and a different template for each order, which breaks grouping. The level comes from the method you call, not from the string, and building the string has nothing to do with thread safety.

quiz.prompt: `logger.LogWarning("Retry {Attempt} for {OrderId}", orderId, attempt)` runs with orderId = 42 and attempt = 3. Which properties are stored?
choices: Attempt = 42 and OrderId = 3
Attempt = 3 and OrderId = 42, matched by name
None: the call throws because the names differ
Only the text, since names are case-sensitive
quiz.explanation: Template placeholders take the arguments in order. The names in braces only label the properties, and the logger never sees your variable names, so it cannot match by name, and nothing throws: the entry is well formed and wrong. Keep the arguments in placeholder order, or let the [LoggerMessage] generator bind by parameter name at compile time.

quiz.prompt: A payment provider call fails, the automatic retry succeeds, and the customer is charged once. Which level fits the line about the failed first attempt?
choices: Critical, because payments matter to the business
Error, because an exception was thrown and caught
Warning: unexpected, but the code handled it
Debug, because the user never noticed anything
quiz.explanation: A level tells the reader what to do. Nothing failed for the customer, so an Error line would send someone to investigate an operation that succeeded, and Critical is for an app or dependency that is down. A handled surprise still deserves a trace in production, which Debug would not leave under the usual Information minimum; a rising count of these lines is the early signal of a struggling provider.

quiz.prompt: The minimum level is Information. What happens on `logger.LogDebug("Cart {Cart}", BuildCartDump())`?
choices: BuildCartDump runs, then the entry is dropped
BuildCartDump never runs, since the call is skipped
The entry is written, since Debug ranks above Information
The call throws, since Debug is switched off
quiz.explanation: C# evaluates every argument before a method body runs, and the level check happens inside the logger, so the dump is built and then thrown away. The compiler skips nothing, Debug ranks below Information, and a disabled level is silent rather than an exception. Guard an expensive argument with logger.IsEnabled(LogLevel.Debug) when it really must be logged.

quiz.prompt: Middleware wraps `await next(context)` in a `BeginScope` holding a CorrelationId. A repository logs three calls deeper, after several awaits. What does its line carry?
choices: Nothing extra, because a scope ends at the first await
The CorrelationId only in lines the middleware writes itself
A fresh CorrelationId generated for each class that logs
The CorrelationId, when the provider includes scopes
quiz.explanation: The scope sits in an async-local slot that flows with the execution context, so it survives awaits and reaches every logger used during the request until the using block ends. It is not tied to the class that opened it, and nothing generates new ids. Whether you see it depends on the provider: the console formatter prints scopes only with IncludeScopes set.

quiz.prompt: A handler calls `logger.LogInformation("Login attempt {Request}", request)`, where `request` is a `record LoginRequest(string Email, string Password)`. What does the message show?
choices: Only the type name, LoginRequest
Every property, the password too
The email only, since Password is a sensitive name
Nothing, since objects are skipped
quiz.explanation: The default formatter renders an object argument with ToString(), and a record's compiler-generated ToString prints each property as Name = value, so the password lands in clear text. Nothing in Microsoft.Extensions.Logging guesses which names are sensitive, and objects are not dropped. Log chosen fields, such as a user id and an outcome, instead of the whole object.

quiz.prompt: A sign-in fails. Which log line is safe to keep for months?
choices: `Sign-in failed for {Email} with password {Password}`
`Sign-in failed; request body {Body}`
`Sign-in failed; Authorization header {Authorization}`
`Sign-in failed for {UserId}: {Reason}`
quiz.explanation: A stable user id and a reason code such as bad-password let you count attacks and help one person without storing anything secret. A wrong password is often a typo of the real one, the body carries that same password, and the Authorization header is a credential that anyone reading the logs could replay. An email is personal data, so it needs a reason of its own.

quiz.prompt: A team hides the headers Authorization and Cookie and logs every other request header. A partner starts sending `X-Api-Key`. What ends up in the log?
choices: Nothing: the key is redacted, since it looks secret
Nothing: the logging middleware rejects the request
The partner's API key, in clear text
Only the header name, with its value dropped
quiz.explanation: A deny-list hides only the names somebody wrote down, so a new credential header is logged as it arrives. No logger inspects values to guess what is secret, and logging never rejects requests. An allow-list fails closed: log the headers you know are safe and write the rest as [Redacted], which is how ASP.NET Core's HTTP logging treats headers outside its RequestHeaders set.

quiz.prompt: A catch block logs a failed payment. Which call stores the stack trace in the entry's exception field?
choices: `logger.LogError(ex, "Payment {PaymentId} failed", paymentId)`
`logger.LogError("Payment {PaymentId} failed", paymentId, ex)`
`logger.LogError("Payment failed: {Error}", ex.Message)`
`logger.LogError($"Payment {paymentId} failed: {ex}")`
quiz.explanation: Only the overload with an Exception parameter fills that field, where the provider keeps type, message and stack trace. Appended after paymentId, ex is a surplus template argument with no placeholder, so the field stays empty. Logging ex.Message drops the stack trace, and the interpolated version also turns the template into one-off text.

quiz.prompt: Startup logs the full `ConnectionStrings:Orders` value so that on-call can see which server the app uses. What is the safer line?
choices: The same value at Debug, which production never turns on
The same value base64-encoded, so nobody reads it at a glance
The same value, but only once at startup
The server and database names parsed from it
quiz.explanation: A connection string usually carries a password or key, and anyone who can read the logs could then reach the database. Parsing it with DbConnectionStringBuilder and logging only the host and database answers the on-call question. Base64 is an encoding anyone can reverse, a Debug line is one config change away from production, and a single startup line is still kept for months.

flashcards.back: Log text with named holes such as {OrderId}: the text stays fixed across calls and each value is stored beside it under that name.
Trace, Debug, Information, Warning, Error, Critical; None switches a category off.
Error: one operation failed and needs a look. Critical: the app or a whole dependency is down and someone must act now.
Says whether a level would be written for this category; check it before computing an argument that costs real work.
The console formatter option that prints scope values; it is off by default, so scopes seem to vanish in a plain console.
One id per request, taken from an incoming header or generated, echoed in the response and attached to each log line through a scope.
Emails, names, addresses and IPs are personal data; logs are copied and kept for months, so prefer a stable internal id.
A source generator attribute on a partial method: it checks the level before boxing values and matches placeholders to parameters at build time.

drills.title: Keep the template, bind the values, add the scope
drills.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Our logs are a wall of text. Every order line is a different string, so we cannot count failures per order, and we cannot pull all the lines of one request. Show me how a structured logger keeps the template, binds the values and adds the correlation id from a scope."

**Why it matters.** Microsoft.Extensions.Logging, Serilog and NLog all work this way: the template is stored as written (it is the grouping key), each placeholder becomes a property, values bind to placeholders by position, and an open scope adds its properties to every line written inside it. A line below the minimum level is dropped before any work is done.

**Your task.** Implement, over the given `LogContext` (minimum level, `Entries`, `Scopes`):
- `void Log(LogContext log, Level level, string template, params object?[] args)`
  - a `level` below `log.Minimum` writes nothing; the minimum itself is written
  - a placeholder is `{Name}` or `{Name:format}`; `{{` and `}}` are a literal `{` and `}`
  - the i-th placeholder takes `args[i]`; a different number of placeholders and arguments throws `ArgumentException`
  - `Message` is the template with each placeholder replaced by its value, formatted with the placeholder's format and the invariant culture when the value is `IFormattable`, else its `ToString()` (`null` renders as `(null)`)
  - `Properties` holds every scope's `(Name, Value)` from outer to inner (an inner scope overwrites an outer one with the same name), then the placeholders' values, which overwrite scope values with the same name
  - add `new LogEntry(level, template, message, properties)` to `log.Entries`, with the template exactly as written
- `IDisposable BeginScope(LogContext log, string name, object? value)`: push the pair onto `log.Scopes` and return a `Scope` whose action removes that pair again

This drill keeps scopes in a plain list. The real `LoggerFactory` keeps them in an async-local slot so that they follow the request across `await`.

**Worked example.** `Log(log, Level.Information, "Order {OrderId} shipped to {Country}", 42, "NL")` inside a scope `CorrelationId = "c-91"` adds an entry with template `Order {OrderId} shipped to {Country}`, message `Order 42 shipped to NL` and properties `CorrelationId = c-91, OrderId = 42, Country = NL`.
hints: The template is the key that groups lines, so it must reach the entry exactly as the caller wrote it, and the values travel beside it under the placeholder names.

Return early below the minimum. Walk the template once, treating doubled braces as text and anything between single braces as a placeholder name up to an optional colon, and pair the n-th placeholder with the n-th argument. Fill the properties from the scopes first and the placeholders last, so later writes win.

Check the level, collect the names and the rendered message in a single pass, refuse a count mismatch, copy the outer to inner scopes and then the call's values into one dictionary, and let the scope handle remove exactly the pair it added.

drills.title: Log a request without its secrets
drills.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Security found bearer tokens and passwords in our log store. The request logger hides `Authorization` and `Cookie` and writes everything else, body included. Rewrite it so that nothing secret or personal gets in, including headers nobody has invented yet."

**Why it matters.** A deny-list hides only what someone thought of, and the next credential header goes straight into the logs. An allow-list fails closed: known-safe values are written, anything else is marked as hidden, so you can still see that it was there. Bodies carry passwords and personal data, so log their length. An email in a route is personal data too.

**Your task.** Implement `IReadOnlyDictionary<string, object?> RequestLogFields(RequestInfo request)`, returning exactly these five fields:
- `"Method"`: the method as it is
- `"Path"`: the path with every match of `LogRules.EmailPattern` replaced by `[email]`
- `"Query"`: a `Dictionary<string, string>` with every query pair; the value is `LogRules.Redacted` when the key is one of `LogRules.SecretQueryKeys`, compared case-insensitively
- `"Headers"`: a `Dictionary<string, string>` with every header under the name it was sent with; the value is kept only when the name is one of `LogRules.AllowedHeaders`, compared case-insensitively, and is `LogRules.Redacted` otherwise
- `"BodyLength"`: the body's number of characters, `0` when there is no body; the body itself is never returned

**Worked example.** The given `SignIn()` request logs `Authorization` and `Cookie` as `[Redacted]`, keeps `Content-Type` and `X-Correlation-Id`, logs `access_token` as `[Redacted]` and `redirect` as `/home`, and gives `BodyLength = 48`.
hints: Ask which fields you know are safe rather than which ones you know are dangerous, because a new header will not be on anyone's list.

Copy the method, mask anything shaped like an email in the path, pass each header through a case-insensitive allow-list and each query value through a case-insensitive secret list, writing the marker for the ones you hide, and record the body's length instead of the body.

Build two case-insensitive sets from the given rules, map every header and query pair to its value or the redaction marker, replace emails in the path with the email marker, and hand back the five fields with a zero length when there is no body.
